paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 5.17 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 6)
paragraphs.text: (a) each of the other parties who is adverse in interest; (b) if the party adverse in interest is a corporation, [certain corporate representatives]; (c) if a litigation representative is appointed for a party, (i) the litigation representative, and (ii) with the Court's permission, the person on whose behalf the litigation representative is appointed if that person is competent to give evidence; … The present form of these rules was recommended by the Alberta Law Reform Institute in its project leading up to the adoption of the new Rules in 2010. They reflect a balancing of the desirability of ensuring full pre-trial disclosure of relevant and material information, with the need to ensure that litigation remains affordable and proportionate to the issues: CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v 801 Seventh Inc, 2023 ABCA 97 at paras. 20-21; Wilbur v Foothills Hospital, 2005 ABCA 220 at paras. 5-7, 50 Alta LR (4th) 203, 367 AR 191. [6] The new Rules both expand and contract the former rules. For example, R. 5.18 codifies the ability developed at common law to question persons who have provided services to a corporation. On the other hand, old R. 201, which allowed questioning of a person “for whose benefit an action is prosecuted”, was not carried forward. The new Rules confirm the long-standing Alberta practice which does not permit the pre-trial questioning of every possible witness: CNOOC at para. 28. The Institute specifically rejected the American practice whereby almost all witnesses can be deposed before trial. [7] Rule 5.17(1)(c), which specifically deals with questioning where a litigation representative has been appointed, is the one most directly applicable in this case. However, while it permits the questioning of the litigation representative and the person he represents, this rule does not provide for the questioning of any other person who might have important information about the litigation. This was a deliberate recommendation of the Institute in its Consultation Memorandum No. 12.4, “Parties”, p. 37, in which it described wider discovery as “excessive”. [8] The new Rules should be interpreted as carrying forward the established rule in Alberta that the right to pre-trial questioning is limited to the persons listed in the rule: see Wilbur at para. 26. This is specifically so with respect to questioning in actions involving litigation representatives, because the rule specifically provides who can be examined in that situation. The general objectives of fairness and efficiency recited in R. 1.2 and 5.1 are interpretive aids, but they cannot override specific limitations built into specific rules. Fairness is found in the consistent application of well defined rules. [9] The appellants argue that the infant plaintiff's mother can be questioned under R. 5.17(1)(a) as an “other party” who is “adverse in interest” because the infant plaintiff has advanced an “in trust” claim to reflect the care given by her mother. The law, however, treats the “in trust” claim as being a claim of the injured plaintiff, not of the person who provided the care: Benstead v Murphy, 1994 ABCA 272 at paras. 25-26, 23 Alta LR (3d) 251, 157 AR 198; Labrecque v Heimbeckner, 2007 ABQB 501at para. 251, 434 AR 181; Forsberg v Naidoo, 2011 ABQB 252 at para. 337, 516 AR 201; K.S. (Litigation Representative of) v Willox, 2016 ABQB 483 at para. 661, 32 CCLT (4th) 1; K.Y. (Litigation representative of) v Bahler, 2023 ABKB 280 at para. 1685. Even if it could be argued that the “in trust” claim will indirectly benefit the mother, that does not make her a party so as to permit questioning her. In any event, this argument would not justify questioning the mother beyond the four corners of the “in trust” claim itself. [10] The appellants also rely on Golden Estate v Neilson, 2011 ABCA 338, 65 Alta LR (5th) 119, 519 AR 165. Golden Estate, however, was a fatal accident claim, which is a form of representative action under which the estate or one dependent can claim on behalf of all dependents of the deceased. Therefore, the mother and spouse of the deceased were described as “true parties” to the action, because they had an independent claim for relief. This decision is not about examining non-parties. [11] Golden Estate suggested: 16 A person for whose benefit an action is prosecuted is regarded as a party to the lawsuit: Re Cantalini and Hirtz. The decision in Re Cantalini (1965), 1965 CanLII 527 (AB KB), 49 DLR (2d) 518 (Alta SC) also concerned a fatal accident claim. Further, both Cantalini at p. 521 and Hirtz v Alberta (Public Trustee), 2000 ABQB 326 at para. 21, 267 AR 52, aff'd 2002 ABCA 29 at para. 1, 99 Alta LR (3d) 1, 303 AR 25 rely on the old Rules that specifically allowed discovery of a person “for whose benefit an action is prosecuted”. As previously noted, these provisions were omitted from the new Rules when they were enacted in 2010. [12] It follows that despite the broad wording used in Golden Estate, it should not be read as holding that any witness who stands to benefit from the action and who has evidence that would enhance speed, economy, fairness and disclosure can be questioned. That would be contrary to the rule that questioning of mere witnesses is not permitted under Alberta practice and would revive the repealed rule that parties for whose benefit the action is being prosecuted can be questioned. [13] While the appellants argue that they do not know the plaintiff's position on liability and quantum, the litigation representative can be questioned under R. 5.17(1)(c). In order to make that an effective process, the litigation representative is obliged to inform himself about relevant and material matters. If the appellants are of the view that the plaintiff's Response to Notice to Admit Facts is deficient, they can pursue the appropriate remedies.[1] Further, the plaintiff's expert reports disclose the factual basis on which those expert opinions are rendered. [14] As noted, the appellants argue that if they are not allowed to question the infant plaintiff's mother they may be subjected to a “trial by surprise”. That, however, is a consequence of the Alberta rule that mere witnesses cannot be questioned. Depending on the nature of the case, the burden of potential “surprise” could fall on either the plaintiff or the defendant. The presence of witnesses with relevant and material information could arise in many types of litigation, but that does not mean that they can all be questioned before trial. If the appellants are taken by surprise they are not without remedy. They could apply for a mid-trial adjournment to make inquiries, or to assemble expert evidence on unexpected issues. They have the option of applying for an adjournment of the trial before closing their case. The management of any such remedies, and the resulting costs, are in the hands of the trial judge. 2. Purpose and Scope (i) Principles In Rainville v. Pontin, 2013 ABQB 256, 2013 CarswellAlta 539, Justice Marceau said, at paragraphs 9-10: 9 Alberta Rules of Court 5.17 states that a party is entitled to ask adverse parties questions under oath about relevant and material records and information. 10 In Suncor Energy Oilsands Limited Partnership v. Propak Systems Ltd., 2012 ABQB 789 at paras. 3–5, Justice Poelman set out the principles for what is now called Questioning: [3] In my view, most of the disputes between these parties over undertaking requests can be determined by basic principles and purposes of the discovery process, now called disclosure and questioning in our rules. [4] The questioning process in an action is fundamentally an inquiry into relevant facts. Further, questions may only seek facts of primary relevance (those directly in issue) or secondary relevance (from which the existence of primary facts may be directly inferred), not tertiary relevance (information that might lead to facts or records of secondary relevance). [5] Furthermore, rule 5.25 (1)(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court provides that “a person is required to answer only … relevant and material questions.” Under rule 5.2 (1)(a), “a question …is relevant and material only if the answer to the question … could reasonably be expected … to significantly help to determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings.” The Court of Appeal elaborated on that definition, as follows: The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990). Facts or documents may be relevant within Rule 186.1, but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving or disproving a fact in issue. As Slatter J. observed in Weatherill Estate v. Weatherill, (2003) 337 A.R. 180 (Q.B.), 2003 ABQB 69 at para. 17, “… relevance is determined by the pleadings while materiality is more a matter of proof …”. See also Tolko Industries Ltd. v. Railink Ltd. (2003), 14 Alta. L.R. (4th) 388, 2003 ABQB 349 at para. 6. (references omitted). (ii) General Rule 200 affords the party opposite an opportunity to discover in advance the evidence to be given at trial by likely witnesses … Because the object of the rule is to force pre-trial disclosure of vital information which is not privileged, the limiting factor in the rule—that the person to be examined have some connection with the party as officer or employee—should be given a wide application. As was said by O'Halloran J.A. in Bell v. Klein[at p. 196], the test: … seems to be whether the person sought to be examined can be regarded as an officer or servant in any permissible sense if he is the one person connected with the company best informed of matters which may define and narrow the issues between the parties at the trial. Cana Construction Co. v. Calgary Centre for Performing Arts (1986), 46 Alta. L.R. (2d) 313 at 315-16 (C.A.). (iii) Special considerations regarding solicitors The Alberta Supreme Court Appellate Division decided in Kirdeikis v Campbell Brothers Real Estate Ltd. (1963), 42 W.W.R. 440 … that a solicitor acting for a client in this professional capacity may not be examined for discovery as an employee of that client … In application of [the principle stated in Cana Construction] we do not find that a solicitor for a corporate litigant who acts only in his capacity as solicitor is a person who has this type of connection with his client, i.e., he or she is not to be considered the one person, connected with the company best informed of matters which may define and narrow the issues between the parties at trial. A solicitor in this position possesses privileged information, pursuant to the solicitor-client privilege arising with his or her litigant client. For this reason the solicitor is not to be considered “an officer … in any permissible sense” as described by O'Halloran J.A. above. He or she falls into the exception to this principle, defined by Kerans J.A. above, by reason of having acquired privileged information. It may be that not all of the solicitor's knowledge about the substance of the litigation is subject to solicitor-client privilege: see United States v. Mammoth Oil Co., [1925] 2 D.L.R. 966 (C.A.). However, because of the potential difficulties in separating privileged from non-privileged information, the solicitor is not to be considered an officer of the company in any permissible sense for the purposes of examination for discovery. Naturally, had the solicitor been acting in an additional or other capacity to that of solicitor to the respondent, the decision would have been different. BTK Holdings Ltd. v. Greater Edmonton Development Corp. (1992), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 78 at 79-80 (C.A.). (iv) “Relevant and material questions” Rule 5.2 sets out a test for “relevance and materiality”. That rule uses the words “could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more issues raised in the pleadings”. Is that a more narrow test than that set by the common law? It is important to note that a question under the rule must be about information that is both “relevant” and “material”. Strictly speaking, those concepts are not synomous, and contribute separate elements to the test. Put simply, a fact is “material” if it assists in proving (or disproving) an issue in the lawsuit. Evidence is “relevant” when it assists in the proving (or disproving) of such a fact. With respect to relevance, in R. v. Cloutier (1979), 28 N.R. 1 (S.C.C.), Pratte J., speaking for the majority, said, at p. 26: For one fact to be relevant to another, there must be a connection or nexus between the two which makes it possible to infer the existence of one from the existence of the other. One fact is not relevant to another if it does not have real probative value with respect to the latter … Doherty J.A., in R. v. Watson (1996), 92 O.A.C. 131 (C.A.), at p. 140 said: Relevance … requires a determination of whether as a matter of human experience and logic the existence of “Fact A” makes the existence or non-existence of “Fact B” more probable than it would be without the existence of “Fact A”. If it does then “Fact A” is relevant to “Fact B”. As long as “Fact B” is itself a material fact in issue or is relevant to a material fact in issue in the litigation then “Fact A” is relevant and prima facie admissible. With respect to materiality, the following two U.S. cases discuss the concept, and its relationship to relevance. In Poulin v. Zartman, 542 P.2d 251 (Alaska S.C. (1975)), Connor J. said, at p. 260: Alaska case law defines the test of relevancy. “To be of sufficient relevance for admission, testimony, documents or other evidence must have some tendency in reason to establish a proposition material to the case.”… The dual concepts of logical relevance, i.e., some tendency to establish the ultimate point for which the evidence is offered, and materiality, i.e., germaneness of the ultimate point to issues in the trial, have been emphasized repeatedly in our opinions. In Azimow (Estate of) v. Azimow, 230 N.E.2d 450 (Ind. App. Ct. (1967)), Smith J., at pp. 451-52, said: To be material, evidence sought by a question must tend to prove or disprove a fact which relates to an issue in the lawsuit … Whereas materiality deals with the relationship between the issues of the case and the fact which the evidence tends to prove, relevancy deals with the requirement that the evidence must logically tend to prove a material fact. In Canada, the concepts of relevance and materiality are often collectively referred to as “relevance”. In Report of the Federal/Provincial Task Force on Uniform Rules of Evidence prepared for the Uniform Law Conference of Canada (1982) the following appears at p. 60: Relevance embraces two distinct reasons for excluding evidence: (a) either the evidence does not tend to prove or disprove the proposition in question; or (b) the proposition to which the party directed the evidence is not in issue in the case. The first reason relates to probative value and involves relevance in its true sense. The second, relating to the issues in the case, involves materiality. Materiality refers to evidence which may be relevant to the proposition for which it is offered, but which is excluded because the proposition is not up for decision in the case. The major issues in a case are defined by substantive law, pleadings and rules of procedure. However, a witness's testimony during the course of the hearing, may open up an issue. Other issues which may arise during the course of the hearing are issues of fact concerning the admissibiltiy of a disputed item of evidence and, on cross-examination of a witness, matters bearing on his credibility. The cases previously decided under former R. 200 stress that the questions may be wide ranging. When dealing with the question of relevance, some of the cases indicate that a question is permissible if it may be relevant to a matter in issue (e.g., Czuy v. Mitchell et al. (1976), 1 A.R. 434, 72 D.L.R. (3d) 424 (C.A.), quoting Turta v. Canadian Pacific Railway). Some of the cases simply speak in terms of relevance (without the qualifying word “may”), but even those cases emphasize the wide scope available to the examiner (e.g., Drake v. Overland (1979), 19 A.R. 472 at 484 (C.A.)). R. 5.17 speaks in terms of questions which are, as opposed to may be, relevant and material. Further, R. 5.2 uses the words “could reasonably be expected” and “significantly help”. These words imply a more narrow test than that which had been developed under the old R. 200. In D'Elia v. Dansereau, 2000 ABQB 425, 2000 CarswellAlta 617, 267 A.R. 157, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 298 ([In Chambers]), Mr. Justice Perras has indicated that in his view the new test is more restrictive. At pp. 301-302, his Lordship said: The ambit for discovery under the previous formulation of the rule relating to oral examination was set by Czuy v. Mitchell. … Hence, the language used to interpret the previous oral discovery rule was very broad and all encompassing. Learned counsel for the plaintiff takes the position that the current formulation of the rule for oral discovery narrows and focusses the scope of oral discovery to those matters that are relevant and material to significantly help determine the issues raised in the pleadings or to ascertain evidence that would do so. … The previous oral discovery rule allowed discovery of parties adverse in interest providing it touched the matters in question. Clearly, the current language in the oral discovery rule has limiting parameters. In my view, it is not enough to argue that questions on discovery “touch the matters in question” but rather, the issue is are the questions relevant and material and, if so, do they advance significantly the determination of the issues raised in the pleadings. Hence, any anaylsis to determine the propriety of disputed questions on oral discovery must start by examining the pleadings. Henceforth the pleadings will be of considerable importance in focussing the issues which in turn will give meaning to materiality and relevance of oral discovery in terms of ascertaining the facts. So, in my view, relevant questions will be those questions having regard to the pleadings that elicit facts that are in issue or facts that make facts in issue, more probable than not. It is my view that the previous broad scope of oral examination is now signficantly narrowed from the previous practice by the reformulation of parts of the discovery rules. In Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation, 2000 ABCA 327, 2000 CarswellAlta 1529, 277 A.R. 138, the Court of Appeal considered the test under the amended rule. The plaintiff brought an action resulting from injuries she allegedly received while participating in a horse jumping event. Before being permitted to engage in the event, she was required to sign a release. She did not plead that she did not sign or understand the release. The defendants pleaded volenti non fit injuria. At examination for discovery the plaintiff refused to answer questions about her previous experience with release forms. The Court of Appeal ordered her to answer the questions. At pp. 140-141, Conrad J.A. said: In arriving at our decision, we note that admissibility and weight are best determined at trial. But for the purpose of discovery, looking at whether Ms. Hepworth had consented to the risk of this event and agreed to waive any claim, it is not unreasonable to examine all of her experience in this kind of equestrian event. That would include the type of risk she would expect to assume and her knowledge and experience with the rules generally in existence. Her prior experience with waivers and releases may go to that issue. It is not merely a question of interpreting the release in question. “Volenti” as a defence does not necessarily involve a written form. Thus, for discovery purposes the facts surrounding the event may be gathered, leaving ultimate admissibility for determination at trial. In our view, it is necessary to look at all of the pleadings when deciding discovery issues. While it is true … that the claim sounds in negligence, paras. 16 and 17 of the statement of claim also plead an agreement, either express or implied, and representations relied upon by the plaintiff as to the fitness of the course. In addition, the claim relies on the experience of Hepworth as a rider with at least 22 years equestrian experience. She has placed her experience in issue by pleading it in her statement of claim. Her past experience may also impact on implied terms, or what the alleged representations are, and whether they were in fact relied upon. In other words, the surrounding circumstances may be relevant to give context to contracts and the plea of representations. What would the plaintiff have reasonably understood was represented? Would her knowledge and experience impact on that?… In determining whether Hepworth consented to the risks involved, the surrounding circumstances will be examined. Furthermore, the validity of issues raised in the pleadings should be left to the trial judge. … Part of the purpose of discovery is to help parties establish what will be in issue at trial. It would seem counterproductive to restrict questions on discovery to those respecting “valid” issues, especially where no impartial decision maker is immediately available to determine the merit or validity of each issue raised. We also note the parites have been given wide latitude in asking questions on discovery. As Fruman J.A., held for the majority in Gienow Building Products Ltd. v. Tremco Inc. et al. (2000), 255 A.R. 273 …: “This court has on numerous occasions observed that the scope of examination for discovery is broad, with relevance or irrelevance being the primary limiting factor.”… The appelleants' questions “touched the matters in question” and were “relevant and material”, as that phrase is defined in the amended Rules. It is interesting to note Conrad, J.A.'s reliance on Gienow Building Products Ltd. v. Tremco Inc. (2000), 255 A.R. 273 when discussing the wide latitude afforded examiners in discovery because Gienow Building Products Ltd. v. Tremco Inc. (2000), 255 A.R. 273 dealt with Rule 200(1) in its form prior to the amendments. However, it is also noteworthy that O'Leary J.A., while in dissent, specifically mentioned the amendments and said: “The amendments do no more than move the words about and add a sub-rule about relevancy. Except with respect to the issues of relevancy, they do not change the scope of examination for discovery of individuals examined on behalf of a corporate party” (p. 290). However, see NAC Constructors Ltd. v. Alberta (Capital Region Wastewater Commission), 2006 ABCA 246, 2006 CarswellAlta 1086, 412 A.R. 272, 63 Alta. L.R. (4th) 19, described below. In 750869 Alberta Ltd. v. Cambridge Shopping Centres Ltd., 2001 ABQB 36, 2001 CarswellAlta 44, 283 A.R. 391, Johnstone J. considered the Court of Appeal's decision in Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation, 2000 ABCA 327, 2000 CarswellAlta 1529, 277 A.R. 138, and found that it was not inconsistent with the movement to limit examinations for discovery. She concluded that Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation, 2000 ABCA 327, 2000 CarswellAlta 1529, 277 A.R. 138 was distinguishable on the ground that the Court of Appeal had found the questions to be “material and relevant”. Her Ladyship then said, at p. 397: I am satisfied from the existing jurisprudence that the intent of the amendment was to limit the scope of discoverability to that of evidence meeting the test of both relevancy and materiality based upon a consideration of all the pleadings. In Johnston v. Bryant, 2003 ABCA 169, 2003 CarswellAlta 763, 327 A.R. 378, 17 Alta. L.R. (4th) 24, Hunt J.A. said, at p. 381: Rule 186.1 is intended to limit the scope of discovery from what it was under previous rules. … The precise scope of this change has not been definitively determined by this court. … In Weatherill Estate v. Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69, 2003 CarswellAlta 81, 337 A.R. 180, 11 Alta. L.R. (4th) 183, Slatter J. commented on the effect of the 1999 amendments. At p. 184, his Lordship said: Examination for discovery now is narrower than it used to be. It is however still quite wide, and is perhaps still wider than the test for admissibility at trial. Certainly discovery is not narrower than admissibility at trial. In interpreting the Rules, the Court should avoid creating an artificial situation where a litigant is not entitled to obtain information on discovery, which the litigant could quite clearly introduce at the trial. In determining whether a document is relevant and material, the starting point is the pleadings. The pleadings define the issues, and relevance must be determined with respect to the issues. The pleadings are also relevant with respect to the issue of materiality. However, with respect to materiality one must also have regard to the issue in question. Where does the burden of proof lie? Is the issue something that is capable of direct proof, or is it something like a person's state of mind, which can only be proven indirectly. Does one party essentially have to try and prove a negative? How are cases of this type usually proven at trial? The less amenable a fact is to direct proof, the wider will be the circle of materiality. There are some facts that can only be proven by essentially eliminating all the competing scenarios, thereby leaving the fact in issue as the sole logical inference. When a state of mind is in issue, it can generally only be proven by demonstrating a pattern of conduct of the person whose state of mind it is. In deciding whether a particular document is material, one must take a very pragmatic view, viewing the situation from the perspective of the party who must prove the fact in question. At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient. Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry. That relevance is determined by the pleadings, while materiality is more a matter of proof can be seen by the wording of the Rule. The Rule talks about records that can “help determine” an issue, or that can “ascertain evidence” that will determine an issue. These are words of proof, and materiality must be determined with that in mind. It is sometimes said that the new Rules prevent the discovery of “tertiary” issues. This is one way of saying that the 1999 amendments were intended to prevent excessive discovery. However, as a working tool the search for “tertiary” issues is unhelpful in many cases. There is no clear dividing line between primary, secondary, and tertiary evidence. As I have indicated, some facts can only be proven by tertiary or even more remote evidence. A good example is an attempt to prove a negative. The application of the new Rule to particular fact situations must be primarily pragmatic. In NAC Constructors Ltd. v. Alberta (Capital Region Wastewater Commission), 2006 ABCA 246, 2006 CarswellAlta 1086, 412 A.R. 272, 63 Alta. L.R. (4th) 19, the Court gave this guidance concerning the scope of discovery (at pp. 23-24): The Rules governing the scope of oral examination for discovery were amended effective November 1, 1999 (A/R 172/99). The obligation of a witness to answer questions on oral examination is now limited to questions seeking evidence that is both “relevant and material” within the meaning of those terms in the Rules. Rule 200(1.2) states in part that: During the oral examination … a person is required to answer only relevant and material questions. New Rule 186.1 defines the concepts of relevance and materiality in relation to oral examination for discovery. It says: For the purpose of this Part, a question … is relevant and material only if the answer to the question … could reasonably be expected (a) to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or (b) to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. In Johnston v. Bryant (2003), 327 A.R. 378, 2003 ABCA 169 (Alta. C.A.), the Court observed at para. 12 that “Rule 186.1 is intended to limit the scope of discovery from what it was under previous rules”. It is “designed to limit … tertiary lines of inquiry”: Auer v. Lionstone Holdings Inc. (2005), 363 A.R. 84, 2005 ABCA 78 30 (Alta. C.A.), citing Hirtz v. Alberta (Public Trustee) (2002), 303 A.R. 25, 2002 ABCA 29 (Alta. C.A.). In Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation (2000), 277 A.R. 138, 2000 ABCA 327 (Alta. C.A.), at para. 12, the Court held the disputed questions were proper under both the new and old discovery Rules. Issues raised in the pleadings are the basis for determining both relevance and materiality: D'Elia v. Dansereau (2000), 267 A.R. 157, 2000 ABQB 425, ¶ 17 (Alta. Q.B. [In Chambers]). Oral examination for discovery is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, that is, facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, that is, facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred. Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings. Questions seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance (that is, questions asking for information that is only of tertiary relevance) need no longer be answered. In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, information sought on discovery must be material, that is, be reasonably expected to “significantly” help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990). Facts or documents may be relevant within Rule 186.1, but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving or disproving a fact in issue. As Slatter J. observed in Weatherill Estate v. Weatherill (2003), 337 A.R. 180, 2003 ABQB 69 (Alta. Q.B.), at para. 17, “… relevance is determined by the pleadings while materiality is more a matter of proof …”. See also Tolko Industries Ltd. v. Railink Ltd. (2003), 14 Alta. L.R. (4th) 388, 2003 ABQB 349, ¶ 6 (Alta. Q.B.). In Alexander v. Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada, 2016 ABQB 445, 2016 CarswellAlta 1501, 58 C.C.L.I. (5th) 117, 88 C.P.C. (7th) 315, Justice Manderscheid gave this summary of the tests used to determine what is relevant and material: 35 In Dow Chemical, [Dow Chemical Canada ULC v. Nova Chemicals Corp. 2014 ABCA 244] at paragraph 17, our Court of Appeal held that, “[a]s the wording of [subrule 5.2(1)] implies, relevance is primarily determined by the pleadings, whereas materiality relates to whether the information can help, directly or indirectly, to prove a fact in issue”. Therefore, I must look to the pleadings to determine whether the Records are relevant, and then assess their materiality. 36 In NAC Constructors Ltd v Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246, [2006] A.J. No 1051 at para 13 (QL), the Court held: The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990). Facts or documents may be relevant within Rule 186.1 [now subrule 5.2(1)], but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving or disproving a fact in issue. 37 Later, in Dow Chemical, at paragraph 19, the Court said, “[t]here is no fixed standard of what is ‘material’. An element of judgment is required”. And, at paragraph 21, the Court held: It is not sufficient for a litigant to show some theoretical line of argument in order to establish “materiality”. The case management judge is fully entitled to reject lines of pretrial discovery that are unrealistic, speculative, or without any air of reality. …[However, at] an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely: Weatherill at para 16. 38 Finally, in the more recent case of Kaddoura, [Royal Bank of Canada v. Kaddoura 2015 ABCA 154] the Court confirmed the statements it made in Dow Chemical and held that, at the production stage of the litigation, a litigant need not “demonstrate conclusively that the discovered records will in fact contain any evidence of assistance to them”; he or she “need only show a plausible line of argument” regarding the probative value of the records he or she seeks: paras 14-15. In Collacutt (Next Friend of) v. Briggs Bros. Student Transportation Ltd., 2008 ABQB 505, 2008 CarswellAlta 1122, 94 Alta. L.R. (4th) 356, Yamuachi J. considered the issue of the scope of the examination between a third party and a defendant. His Lordship set out the facts at p. 359: 1 The Plaintiff was struck by a school bus operated by Dorothy Colleen Bondarchuk (the “Applicant”) and owned by Briggs Bros. Student Transportation Ltd. (collectively, the “Defendants”). The Plaintiff's parents are the Third Parties in this action. The Plaintiff has filed discontinuances of action against the other defendants. 2 On February 8, 2008, Applicant's counsel was conducting an oral examination for discovery of Vivian Collacutt in her capacity as a Third Party (the “Respondent”). Applicant's counsel asked the Respondent a question concerning the Plaintiff's damages, to which the Respondent's counsel objected and instructed the Respondent not to answer the question. The Applicant makes this application to determine whether the Respondent must answer questions concerning the Plaintiff's damages. This is a question which may depend on the evidence led at trial, as well as upon the proper interpretation of s. 27. We were urged, however, to consider relevancy on the basis of the Bank's view of the correct interpretation of s. 27. It was alleged the section gave the Bank the exclusive power to determine whether an offer was bona fide in the sense that the offeror was making a realistic offer to purchase and therefore the question of his identity was irrelevant. It may mean that in retrospect the identity of the offeror was not material, but that conclusion cannot be reached at this stage of the proceedings. The irony of such a situation is apparent but it is not different from many cases where the evidence is allowed subject to later determination as to its relevancy. After all, what is relevant is often not apparent during trial as that determination is dependent on the ultimate conclusion reached by the trial judge.
